data.title: India, Iran hold bilateral talks on cultural cooperation during SCO forum
data.description:
India and Iran held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum to bolster cultural cooperation, Union Culture Secretary Vivek Aggarwal said on Sunday.

At a press interaction held at the venue, the historic Purana Quila, shortly before the closure of the session, asked if any formal bilateral talks were held between India and Pakistan on the sidelines, Aggarwal said, "There were no formal bilateral talks between the two sides." However, he said that members of the Indian side did have interactions with him over banquets and during the conference, as well as there were other "informal discussions" with him during the course of the forum, as with other ministers too.

 

"In general, there were also meetings between ministers and heads of delegations, as the aim of this (multilateral) forum is to exchange views, so there were many meetings, and a lot of things were discussed," the culture secretary said.

However, he didn't specify how many bilateral talks took place during the course of the Forum hosted by India from November 20-22.

Asked if any bilateral meeting took place with Iran, he said, "There was a bilateral meeting with Iran. And India is in constant touch with Iran, and on areas in which there can be any cultural exchange, we are always in discussion. And discussions took place during the Summit too." The secretary said that during the bilateral meeting, "ideas have been thrown, though no such project has been concretised yet. But the discussions and engagements are on".

The three-day event was hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs.

The Iranian Embassy in India in a post on X on Sunday said, at the civilisational summit, Tehran proposed setting up an "SCO Joint Network for Written Heritage and Civilisational Memory".

Dr Faridoddin Faridasr, Cultural Counsellor of the Islamic Republic of Iran in India, addressed the First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi, highlighting the importance of shared civilisational heritage as a foundation for cultural cooperation and mutual understanding among SCO member states, it said.

In his remarks, he emphasised the historical role of the "Persian language as a language of science, literature, administration and cultural exchange across Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and neighbouring regions, describing it as an important part of the shared cultural and historical heritage of the region".

Referring to Iran's successful cultural cooperation with India, he highlighted the activities of the Noor International Microfilm Centre, affiliated with the Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in New Delhi. Since 1990, the Centre has collaborated with 72 academic and cultural institutions in India, resulting in the digitisation of "more than 150,000 Persian and Arabic manuscripts," the restoration and preservation of over three million pages of historical documents, and the preparation of nearly 300 catalogues, the embassy said.

Faridasr also referred to the ongoing joint projects with cultural institutions in Telangana and Hyderabad for the digitisation, restoration and preservation of historical Persian documents and manuscripts.

As a practical initiative to strengthen regional cultural cooperation, he proposed the establishment of an "SCO Joint Network for Written Heritage and Civilizational Memory." "The proposed network would focus on the preservation and digitisation of manuscripts and historical documents, the exchange of technical expertise and training in manuscript restoration, and the promotion of shared linguistic and literary heritage through joint research, publications and exhibitions," the embassy said in a detailed post on X.

He reaffirmed Iran's "readiness to share its experience and technical expertise with other SCO member states", stressing that the preservation of shared civilisational heritage provides an important opportunity to strengthen mutual trust, cultural understanding and cooperation across the region.

The forum was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 20. It saw the participation of delegates from various Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member countries, including Pakistan, and other countries.

data.title: El Nino may trigger floods, landslides in Hindu Kush Himalaya: Report
data.description:
A strong El Nino could bring above-normal precipitation to parts of the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, increasing the risk of floods, landslides and avalanches in Nepal during the winter season, according to a report.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) Winter Outlook 2026, jointly prepared by the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), Beijing Normal University and the Institute of Atmospheric Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, forecasts wetter conditions in countries including Nepal, Afghanistan and Bangladesh.

The report warns that heavy precipitation could trigger localised floods, landslides and avalanches in the western Himalaya, while some parts of the region may experience dry spells and an increased risk of forest fires.

 

The outlook comes as the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reports a strong-to-very-strong El Nino, with around a 60 per cent chance of it becoming the strongest since records began in 1950.

ICIMOD scientists said the weather phenomenon could bring more rain to the Himalayan foothills and increased snowfall at higher elevations.

The report follows a particularly destructive monsoon season in Nepal and Bhutan, marked by disasters linked to changes in high-mountain glaciers and permafrost.

The devastating Bhotekoshi floods that struck the Himalayan nation in August, killing at least 1,500 people and leaving over 5,000 missing, are estimated to have cost the country USD 4.7 billion in relief and reconstruction.

The outlook also forecasts deeper-than-normal snow in parts of Afghanistan, Pakistan, northern India and Nepal, while shallower snow levels are expected in parts of Bhutan and eastern Xizang in China.

Snow depth plays a crucial role in sustaining river flows and determining water availability for the coming year. Lower snow levels could affect irrigation, hydropower generation and spring flows, the report said.

"A wetter winter does not rule out the risk of fire, as other regions in the HKH are expected to face dry spells, leaving grass and other vegetation dry enough to burn," the report warned.

It also projected a high to very high likelihood of forest and grassland fires in southeastern Xizang and parts of Myanmar.

"Preparedness cannot end with the monsoon. As rainfall becomes more erratic and intense, local authorities need seasonal outlooks to plan and short-range local forecasts to decide when and where to act," said Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at ICIMOD.

ICIMOD will discuss the findings at an international conference titled Advancing Science, Policy and Regional Cooperation for the HKH Cryosphere, scheduled to be held in Kathmandu from November 25 to 27.

data.title: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes industry limits on AI development
data.description:
By Jorgelina do Rosario
 
OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behavior.
 
Jakub Pachocki called for industrywide standards that would establish thresholds for AI development, with companies agreeing not to exceed them until specific safety requirements are met, according to a post published Sunday.
 
“I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone,” Pachocki wrote.
 
The proposed limits could be based partly on a technical measurement known as perplexity, which gauges how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. Pachocki didn’t specify what the initial limit should be or when it might take effect.
 
 
Pachocki warned that AI could accelerate advances in its own development as soon as 2027, potentially outpacing improvements in researchers’ ability to monitor and understand the technology.
 
OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman endorsed the proposal, calling Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile.” He said in a post on X that agreeing to common limits would help ensure “safety and control.”
 
The proposal comes as the US prepares for renewed debate over AI regulation following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections. The party’s gains in the House, Senate and governors’ races could bring greater congressional scrutiny of technology companies and renewed efforts to establish AI safety rules.
 
Some lawmakers are also discussing the creation of a dedicated Senate committee to coordinate AI policy. President Donald Trump has opposed broad restrictions on AI development, setting up a potential clash with the incoming Democratic Congress over how to regulate the technology.

data.title: Delhi air quality remains poor as AQI rises, forecast signals no respite
data.description:
Delhi’s air quality remained in the ‘poor’ category on Monday, with the city recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 248 at 7 am, according to real-time data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). PM2.5 continued to be the prominent pollutant.
 
The city-level reading was 12 points higher than the AQI of 236 reported at 9 am on Sunday. Pollution levels varied considerably across the capital. Of the 58 monitoring stations with valid readings at 7 am, 51 recorded AQI levels above 200, while five reported readings above 300, placing them in the ‘very poor’ category.
 
Sirifort recorded the highest AQI at 331, followed by NSUT Jaffarpur at 323 and IGNOU, Maidan Garhi, at 320. Talkatora Garden reported 315, while Pusa, monitored by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), recorded 312.
 
 
Among other locations, ITO recorded an AQI of 297, CRRI Mathura Road 296, Aya Nagar 295 and Burari Crossing 293. Commonwealth Sports Complex reported 291, while DTU recorded 288.
 
At the other end, Ghoga recorded the lowest AQI at 130, followed by Lodhi Road at 149 and IMD Lodhi Road at 161. These locations were in the ‘moderate’ category.

NCR cities report mixed air quality

Air quality across the National Capital Region (NCR) remained uneven. Rohtak in Haryana recorded an AQI of 248, the same as Delhi, while Ghaziabad reported 233 and Bhiwadi in Rajasthan 229.
 
Greater Noida recorded an AQI of 228, followed by Manesar at 217, Hapur at 216, Gurugram at 215 and Noida at 212. Bahadurgarh reported 197, while Meerut recorded 187.
 
Among other NCR cities, Bulandshahr reported an AQI of 178, Sonipat 174 and Baghpat 168. Faridabad recorded 136, while Bharatpur and Alwar reported 127 and 124, respectively. Panipat and Palwal were among the better-performing locations, with readings of 95 and 94.

Hanumangarh, Malegaon record highest AQI nationally

Among the 281 cities with valid readings in the CPCB’s 7 am dataset, Hanumangarh in Rajasthan and Malegaon in Maharashtra recorded the highest AQI at 276 each. Panchgaon in Haryana followed at 265, while Dharuhera recorded 264 and Bhiwani 261.
 
Udaipur in Rajasthan reported an AQI of 260, followed by Bikaner at 256. Rohtak and Delhi both recorded 248, while Khairthal in Rajasthan also reported 248. Gajraula in Uttar Pradesh recorded 241.
 
At the other end, Aizawl in Mizoram recorded the lowest AQI at 9, followed by Sasaram in Bihar at 17 and Gangtok in Sikkim at 27. Begusarai in Bihar reported 30, while Rairangpur in Odisha recorded 34. Ramgarh in Bihar, Gaya in Bihar and Bhilai in Chhattisgarh reported readings of 35 each.
 
Under the CPCB’s National Air Quality Index classification, readings between 0 and 50 are categorised as ‘good’, 51 and 100 as ‘satisfactory’, 101 and 200 as ‘moderate’, 201 and 300 as ‘poor’, 301 and 400 as ‘very poor’, and 401 and 500 as ‘severe’.

Forecast points to continued poor air quality

The latest available forecast from the Air Quality Warning and Integrated Decision Support System for Emissions - Delhi (AIRWISE-Delhi) indicates that the capital’s air quality is likely to remain in the ‘poor’ category from Monday to Wednesday, with the possibility of readings moving between ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ over the following six days. Favourable winds and an increase in mixing depth had helped disperse pollutants over the weekend, but the improvement may not be sustained, according to a report by India Today citing the forecast.
 
The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) currently lists Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap) as active across Delhi-NCR. Under Stage II of Grap, measures including mechanised road sweeping, dust suppression, water sprinkling are taken along with stricter enforcement of dust-control norms at construction sites and restrictions on the use of personal vehicles.

data.title: Trump's description of Putin as a friend is entirely appropriate: DNI chief
data.description:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday it was "entirely appropriate" for President Donald Trump to call Russian leader Vladimir Putin his friend.

Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterized as a betrayal of American values after Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for rare three-way talks. The summit last week in China seemed to be more symbolism than substance, but Trump and his top aides have described it as a historic gathering of the three countries with the largest nuclear arsenals.

Trump raised eyebrows with his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his "friend," which continued on Saturday, when the Republican president posted an image on Truth Social of him shaking hands with a smiling Putin under the caption, "My Friend." "In that circle - in that circle of that conversation, using the term friend' is entirely appropriate," Clayton said on ABC's "This Week." He had a similar assessment on CNN's "State of the Union," where he said it was "historic" and "remarkable" for Trump to meet with the presidents of the other leading nuclear powers.

 

"In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely," Clayton said.

Like Trump, Clayton declined when pressed to characterize Putin as a friend of the United States, noting Russia's invasion of Ukraine, an American ally.

"He is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all," Clayton said on ABC.

Trump's fondness for Putin has been a defining characteristic of Trump's two terms as president. He beamed when meeting the Russian leader last week. After returning to Washington, Trump made no effort in the White House briefing room on Friday to walk back the comments, and he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the US.

"I can't speak to America," Trump said, then immediately shifted to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good." Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York criticized the summit as a "historic embarrassment" for the United States.

"America would have been far better off if Trump just stayed home," Schumer said from the Senate floor.

data.title: Democrats clinch biggest House majority since 1992 with at least 258 seats
data.description:
House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

 

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome." Election rout creates a mandate to governThe numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change." Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people - and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?" The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations - a standard oversight function of Congress - may amount to "blatant criminality." A new generation of leadersAfter House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority - meaning any few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda - the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith - people come to the caucus with different ideas - it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's highwater marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Tata Steel, Waaree, Adani Energy, Maruti, IndusInd Bank
data.description:
Stocks to watch today: GIFT Nifty indicated a positive start for domestic indices on Monday as it traded 167.5 points, or 0.65 per cent, lower at 25,913 as of 07:42 AM.
 
Earlier on Friday, the Nifty 50 index closed 26.30 points, or 1.12 per cent, higher at 25,800.60. The 30-share BSE Sensex rallied 897.96 points, or 1.08 per cent, to settle at 83,919.71.
 
Meanwhile, Asian stocks were trading mixed, defying Friday’s moves on Wall Street. At the last check, South Korea's Kospi index was down 4.25 per cent, while Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 4.59 per cent. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded 0.08 per cent higher.
 
 
Overnight in the US, all three key Wall Street indices closed sharply lower. The Dow Jones Industrial Average tanked 1.93 per cent, the S&P 500 lost 3.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28 per cent.
 
Oil prices stayed below $95 per barrel. Brent crude’s December futures were quoting at $92.29, down 0.30 per cent. WTI crude fell 0.22 per cent to $83.23 per barrel.
 
Stocks to watch
 
Tata Steel: The company has approved the sale of its tubes business and entire stake in Tata Steel Colours to APL Apollo Tubes in transactions valued at up to ₹28,000 crore, subject to regulatory clearances, with completion expected by March 2028. Waaree Energies: Its wholly owned subsidiary, Waaree Forever Energies, has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with SECI for a 700 MW solar project in Solapur, Maharashtra. The project also includes a 700 MW/2,800 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS).
 
Adani Energy Solutions: Subsidiary Powerpulse Trading Solutions has received a Letter of Award from WBSEDCL to supply 1,750 MW of round-the-clock renewable energy, along with an additional 750 MW under a greenshoe option.
 
Maruti Suzuki: The company has announced price hikes across select models with immediate effect. The weighted average increase is around 0.31 per cent to partially offset sustained input cost pressures.
 
IndusInd Bank: The bank’s board has decided to terminate former MD and CEO Sumant Kathpalia’s employment with immediate effect following an enquiry. It has also invoked applicable malus and clawback provisions retrospectively from March 24, 2020.
 
Premier Explosives: The company has secured an international export order worth $33.60 million (around ₹311 crore) for the manufacturing and supply of defence explosives.
 
RVNL: The company has emerged as the lowest bidder (L1) for a ₹348.49 crore East Coast Railway order to augment the Vadlapudi Wagon Workshop in Visakhapatnam.
 
Ratnaveer Precision Engineering: The company has secured long-term orders covering nearly 50 per cent of its upcoming copper clad laminate (CCL) manufacturing capacity. Its ₹338 crore capex project targets ₹750 crore in annual revenue and ₹150 crore in EBITDA at full capacity, with commercial production expected from February 2027.
 
Texmaco Rail & Engineering: The company has received two domestic letters of intent worth a combined ₹230.58 crore from JSW Group entities for manufacturing and supplying 553 wagons.
 
Aurobindo Pharma: The USFDA has issued an Establishment Inspection Report (EIR) with a Voluntary Action Indicated (VAI) classification for subsidiary Apitoria Pharma’s API facility, formally closing the August 2026 inspection that had resulted in three observations.
 
Cohance Lifesciences: The USFDA has issued an EIR with a VAI classification for its formulation manufacturing facility in Shamshabad, Telangana, formally concluding the earlier inspection.
 
Welspun Living: The company’s board has approved capital expenditure of up to ₹3,200 crore through its subsidiary, Welspun Home Solutions.
 
Arvind: The company has partnered with unspun to become the first manufacturer to deploy its OneWeave 3D weaving technology.
 
NATCO Pharma: The USFDA inspection at its Kothur facility in Hyderabad has concluded with seven Form 483 observations.

Nifty tech view

The Nifty50 commenced the week on a relatively subdued note, but buying momentum gathered significant traction during the final couple of sessions, propelling the index towards the 25800 mark. data.title: SCO issues Indraprastha Communique, calls for respect for all civilisations
data.description:
The SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum hosted by India on Sunday came out with an outcome document -- Indraprastha Communique -- which called for the protection of cultural heritage, including from illicit trafficking, and "respecting every civilisation as an equal voice".

The three-day forum at the Purana Qila was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 20. It saw the participation of delegates from various Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member countries, including Pakistan's federal minister Musadik Malik.

The Communique begins with a text: "Member States and Dialogue Partners of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), assembled at 'Purana Qila' in New Delhi for the First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, having held harmonious, constructive and meaningful deliberations".

 

It further says that they are cognisant that societies of the SCO countries have been shaped by centuries of interaction, exchange of ideas, movement of people, and sharing of knowledge, while "preserving their distinct identities, cultures, traditions and beliefs".

The Communique is named after the ancient moniker of the region where the Purana Qila is situated.

Member States and Dialogue Partners of the SCO in the outcome document have reaffirmed their collective commitment, founded on "mutual trust, harmony, equality, consultation, and respect for civilisational diversity and pursuit of sustainable development", and guided by these principles, "culture was recognised as a vital bridge of friendship and good-neighbourliness among the nations", and an important dimension of cooperation envisaged under the SCO Charter.

The Communique also recognised that cultural heritage encompasses monuments, manuscripts, literature, works of art, living traditions, cuisine, performing arts, creative endeavours and knowledge-systems passed on through generations.

Union Culture Secretary Vivek Aggarwal read the Communique at the closing session of the Forum which was hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs from November 20-22, with Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) as the knowledge partner.

Asked how will the vision laid out in the document will be translated into action, Aggarwal said the SCO has a permanent Secretariat, and the Communique will be shared with the Secretariat. Then any action will be taken in conjunction with the SCO, he said.

Asked if there was concurrence of all members, the secretary said, it is "not exactly a negotiated document, it is an outcome document", which is an outcome of this Forum, and lays a "roadmap for future course of action".

The SCO Forum document also called for protection of heritage, including cultural properties from illicit trafficking, and from natural calamities.

The Communique also advocated embracing technology and "constructive use of artificial intelligence" in accessing cultural heritage.

It also affirmed "respecting every civilisation as an equal voice, and acknowledging its identity and contribution to humanity".

It recognised shared legacies in architecture, music, cuisine and textiles.

The Communique also underlined joint nomination by countries for UNESCO heritage tag.

Asked if the subject of joint nomination came up for discussions during the forum, including from Pakistan side, Aggarwal said, "As a principle, it has been discussed, but which countries will join, what nomination will be taken up, that will depend on future discussions that will happen".

Asked if the Communique was equivalent to a joint statement, and if there was concurrence of all members, Alok Dimri, Additional Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs, and National Coordinator for the SCO, said, "It's a matter of technicality, as this is an SCO event, but we have dialogue partners also participating. So, in SCO parlance, typically a joint statement is done by member states. But, nonetheless, it encapsulates the proceedings, and codifies it in the form a document." Asked why the name Indraprastha was chosen for the Communique, Aggarwal said, "The name of the place, where we are sitting, is known as 'Indraprast' in the revenue records also of Delhi. We have shown an artifact here carrying an inscription which mentions 'Indraprastha'".

The SCO was founded at a summit in Shanghai in 2001 by the presidents of Russia, China, the Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

India and Pakistan became its permanent members in 2017. Iran became a member in 2023.

Scholars, academics, experts and cultural representatives gathered for the three-day event to explore the "shared civilisational heritage of SCO countries".

The initiative builds upon the proposal made by PM Modi at the SCO Summit in Tianjin, China, in 2025 to establish a dedicated platform for civilisational dialogue under the SCO framework. The proposal was subsequently welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration of the SCO.

After inaugurating the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, Prime Minister Modi had emphasised the significance of holding a dialogue on civilisational connections in India at a time when global discussions are "dominated by war and unrest", asserting that cultural connections serve as the "strongest guarantee" for world peace.

In his address, he also noted that cultural and civilisational cooperation among member countries of the SCO can further strengthen these ties.

data.title: Delta Airlines' automation system glitch triggers widespread flight delays
data.description:
Over a thousand Delta Air Lines' flights were delayed on Sunday after an automated system that calculates an aircraft's weight malfunctioned during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

The airline said Sunday morning that its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they sought to restore the automation system that ensures an aircraft isn't too heavy to fly. Hours later, Delta said that system was once again working, though flights were still not back to normal.

The airline said it was helping passengers who needed hotel rooms or meals but hoped to have all the delayed flights in the air by the end of the day.

 

On Sunday morning, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hour-long ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta's hub and one of the busiest airports in the world.

Complying with the weight and balance limits of an aircraft is critical to flight safety, according to an FAA document, and going above the limit can compromise the structural integrity of the aircraft.

The agency said on X that the delays weren't related to FAA air traffic systems.

Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage -- forcing it to delay departing flights.

The Delta delays come as Americans have been encountering a growing number of problems with technology that are increasingly disrupting their lives. And the disruptions came just days before the Thanksgiving holiday, the busiest travel season in the United States.

As of Sunday evening, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 58 per cent, or about 2,000, of Delta's flights were delayed; it wasn't immediately clear how many of those involved flights into or out of the Atlanta airport.

FlightAware said that about 58 per cent of flights out of the Atlanta airport were delayed while about 50 per cent of flights destined for the airport were delayed. The vast majority of flights at the Atlanta airport are operated by Delta.

Delta said about 70 per cent of the delays and cancellations noted by FlightAware were connected to the automation issue and the rest were because of inclement weather.

By mid-afternoon, Delta was apologising for the delays, and said it was rebooking customers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed, and offering refunds if a flight was cancelled. According to FlightAware, 3 per cent of the airline's flights were cancelled.
